title: Moncrieff and Hood disappearance
summary: A Ryan B-1 Brougham attempting the first trans-Tasman flight from Australia to New Zealand departed Richmond with four occupants on January 10, 1928. The aircraft carried extra fuel tanks that precluded pilot relief throughout the 20-hour flight. Radio signals were received for 12 hours, but radio contact was lost and the aircraft disappeared over the Tasman Sea. Despite searches and purported sightings, no trace was found.

factors.evidence: Extra fuel tank installed in cabin precluded any chance of pilots changing places in the air, restricting control to one person for flight duration.
The trans-Tasman route was untested at the time and represented a pioneering long-distance ocean crossing.
During a test flight to Richmond, radio not working at all; pilots believed they were sending messages but were not.
Radio contact lost after 12 hours; aircraft disappeared with no trace found despite searches.

events.text: Engine started at 02:00 Sydney time on Tuesday 10 January 1928 for trans-Tasman flight.
Aircraft departed Sydney with four occupants for approximately 1430 mile Tasman crossing to New Zealand.
Radio signals received from aircraft for 12 hours after departure indicating aircraft was airborne and functioning.
Radio contact was lost after approximately 12 hours of flight; aircraft did not respond to subsequent calls.

notes: Text provides extensive background but limited accident details; no investigation findings or cause determination; loss of control inferred from disappearance but mechanism unknown; pioneering flight with untested route

title: 1928 KLM Fokker F.III Waalhaven crash
summary: A KLM Fokker F.III operating a sightseeing flight from Waalhaven Airport in Rotterdam stalled shortly after takeoff during a strong wind gust. The pilot, Scott, had been trained on the more modern Fokker F.VII and F.VIIa aircraft but received only brief training for the F.III, which was a difficult aircraft to fly under crosswind conditions. The aircraft drifted right due to the wind, struck boats in Waalhaven harbor with its landing gear and right wing, and plunged into the water. One of five female passengers drowned after not using the emergency hatch, though investigation concluded all passengers could have survived had they known of and used the ceiling exit.
probable_cause: The aircraft stalled shortly after taking off due to a sudden wind gust that made the aircraft bank. The pilot's insufficient training on the Fokker F.III, which required careful handling under difficult conditions, contributed to the loss of control.

factors.evidence: Schott was trained for the more modern Fokker F.VII and Fokker F.VIIa airplanes and only had a brief training session for the F.III type
The Fokker F.III required a well-trained pilot as it was difficult to fly under the said conditions
A sudden wind gust made the aircraft bank towards the north side of the airfield
The aircraft stalled shortly after taking off with a low-hanging tail in abnormal position
The passengers had not known the location of the emergency hatch in the ceiling of the aircraft

events.text: After the usual test of the engine, the plane departed at 2:48 p.m. local time in a westerly direction.
After 150 meters in the air, the airplane flew in an abnormal position with a low-hanging tail; a sudden wind caused the aircraft to drift to the right.
The aircraft stalled just over the fence of the airport.
The main landing gear and right wing struck boats at the Waalhaven harbor; the plane glided seventy-five meters into the water where it sank.

notes: Investigation recommended better pilot-aircraft type assignment procedures and passenger briefing on emergency exits

title: 1928 Dornier J Santos Dumont crash
summary: On 3 December 1928, two Dornier Do J seaplanes, P-BAIA Guanabara and P-BACA Santos Dumont, took off from Guanabara Bay and flew over the SS Cap Arcona to send welcome messages to aviation pioneer Alberto Santos Dumont. Due to the error of one of the pilots, the two aircraft entered a collision course. The Guanabara escaped unscathed from the near collision, but the Santos Dumont crashed into Guanabara Bay, watched by the crew and passengers of the Arcona. Only the mechanic Walter Hasseldorf initially survived the crash but died hours later. During removal of bodies and aircraft remains, a Brazilian Navy diver also died.
probable_cause: Due to the error of one of the pilots, the two aircraft entered a collision course, forcing the pilots to perform evasive maneuvers.

factors.evidence: Due to the error of one of the pilots, the two aircraft entered a collision course, forcing the pilots to perform evasive maneuvers.
The Santos Dumont crashed into Guanabara Bay.

events.text: The Dornier Do Js P-BAIA Guanabara and P-BACA Santos Dumont took off from Guanabara Bay and flew over the Cap Arcona.
Due to the error of one of the pilots, the two aircraft entered a collision course, forcing the pilots to perform evasive maneuvers.
The Santos Dumont crashed into Guanabara Bay, watched by the crew and passengers of the Arcona and Alberto Santos Dumont.

notes: Limited investigation detail in historic event; cause stated as pilot error causing collision course.
